body:
Prevention begins before construction

Land-use planning is one of the most effective ways to reduce exposure to landslides. In highly susceptible areas, authorities may restrict unsuitable development, require detailed site investigations or keep buildings and essential facilities away from dangerous slopes and potential landslide paths.

Regional susceptibility maps help identify areas needing attention. Detailed decisions about a particular building site or road section require more local information because terrain conditions may change over short distances.

Basic slope-protection approaches

Protecting natural support

Avoiding unnecessary cutting at the foot of a slope can help preserve its support. Road construction, quarrying and excavation require appropriate assessment and control. Dumping large quantities of spoil or other material on unstable slopes may increase loading and should be avoided.

Managing water

Surface water should be directed away from vulnerable locations through properly planned and maintained drainage. Blocked drains, uncontrolled runoff and leaking water systems may increase infiltration and erosion. Drainage measures should be designed for the actual site; simply transferring water to another unstable slope can create a new problem.

Maintaining vegetation and soil cover

Suitable vegetation and soil-conservation measures can help protect shallow slopes from erosion and some forms of instability. Revegetation is especially useful when combined with sound drainage and land-use practices. It cannot replace geological assessment where a deep or large rock mass is unstable.

Protective works

At selected sites, qualified agencies may use retaining structures, protective barriers, rockfall protection and other stabilisation measures. Their suitability depends on the material, movement type and local conditions. These measures should not be treated as universal remedies for every landslide.

Recognising possible warning signs

Some unstable slopes show observable changes before failure. These may include fresh or widening ground cracks, unusual settlement, newly tilted trees or poles, increasing seepage, small rockfalls or unexpected movement of soil. Such signs justify caution and prompt reporting, although their absence does not prove that a slope is safe.

Public precautions during periods of heightened danger

  • Follow official rainfall alerts, landslide warnings, road closures and evacuation instructions.
  • Avoid unnecessary travel along steep, unstable mountain roads during severe weather.
  • Do not stand below cracked rock faces, active landslide scars or slopes where stones are falling.
  • Move away from visibly unstable ground and potential debris-flow channels when danger is apparent.
  • Report fresh cracks, rockfalls, blocked drainage or slope movement to the local administration or responsible road authority.
  • Do not enter a damaged road or landslide area merely because the initial movement has stopped; further movement may occur.

Institutional responsibilities

GSI provides geological investigations, susceptibility information and landslide-related forecasting. Road and infrastructure agencies are responsible for managing the safety of their assets. State Disaster Management Authorities and District Disaster Management Authorities coordinate wider preparedness, warnings, response and recovery within their jurisdictions. The NDMA provides national policy direction and guidelines.

In Gujarat, the same principles apply to local hill roads and settlements where slope conditions require attention, including suitable sites in the Dangs and other hilly areas. Decisions should follow local assessments rather than assumptions based only on the state's overall geography.

Prelims focus

  • Land-use control reduces exposure to unstable slopes.
  • Drainage management helps prevent water-related weakening of slopes.
  • Vegetation assists shallow slope protection but cannot prevent every deep-seated landslide.
  • Road excavation and dumping can destabilise slopes.
  • Trap: A retaining structure or tree plantation is not a universal substitute for site-specific assessment.

[Sources: NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, chapter 6, Natural Hazards and Disasters, section Mitigation of Landslides; NDMA, Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches, June 2009, chapters on mitigation, monitoring and preparedness; GSI, official Landslide Hazard guidance, consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Reducing Landslide Risk Through Land-Use Planning and Public Preparedness

body:
What is a snow avalanche?

A snow avalanche is the rapid downslope movement of a mass of snow under gravity. It may contain ice, rock fragments, soil or vegetation picked up during movement. Avalanches occur primarily in mountainous regions where enough snow accumulates on slopes capable of releasing it.

The visible starting point may be high on a mountain, but the moving snow can travel a considerable distance downhill. Roads, camps, settlements and other infrastructure in the lower part of an avalanche path can therefore be exposed even if the snow does not release immediately above them.

How snow becomes unstable

Snow accumulates in layers as successive snowfalls and weather changes alter the snowpack. Layers may differ in hardness, density, temperature and bonding. Some layers or interfaces are relatively weak. When the weight and forces acting on a snow mass exceed its resistance to movement, a portion of the snowpack may detach.

Instability does not depend only on the total depth of snow. The arrangement and strength of layers are important. A fresh heavy snowfall may add weight to an existing weak layer, while wind can redistribute snow and produce concentrated deposits on certain slopes.

Loose-snow and slab avalanches

TypeHow movement beginsCharacteristic appearance
Loose-snow avalancheRelatively uncohesive snow begins moving from a limited point or area.The moving mass may widen as it descends and collects more snow.
Slab avalancheA more cohesive plate of snow breaks away, commonly above a weak layer.A substantial section of the snowpack can release together.

Avalanches can also be described as dry or wet, depending on the moisture condition of the snow. A wet avalanche may be associated with melting conditions or rain affecting the snowpack, while dry-snow avalanches can occur in cold conditions.

Important avalanche triggers

  • Heavy snowfall: Adds new weight to the snowpack, especially when deposited rapidly.
  • Wind loading: Transports snow and builds deposits that may be unstable.
  • Temperature change: Can alter the strength and bonding of snow layers; warming may favour wet-snow instability.
  • Rain on snow: Introduces liquid water and can change snowpack stability.
  • Disturbance: Movement over an unstable slope, seismic shaking or another disturbance can initiate failure under suitable conditions.

Avalanches can occur after snowfall has stopped. Clear weather alone does not establish that a previously loaded snow slope has become safe.

A snow avalanche is movement of snow. A debris avalanche is a rapid mass movement of earth materials. Both are gravity-driven, but their principal materials and conditions are different.

Prelims focus

  • Snow avalanches involve gravity-driven movement of snow.
  • Loose-snow and slab avalanches are 2 basic types identified in NDMA's 2009 guidelines.
  • A weak layer beneath a cohesive snow slab can contribute to slab release.
  • Heavy snowfall, wind loading and temperature changes influence avalanche instability.
  • Trap: Avalanches may occur after snowfall has ended.

[Sources: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches, June 2009, section 1.7, The Snow Avalanche Hazard, especially section 1.7.2, Types of Avalanches.]

pictures.caption: A snow avalanche descending from a high Himalayan slope towards the valley below.

title: Snow Avalanches: Formation, Types and Triggering Conditions

body:
The 3 functional parts of an avalanche path

An avalanche path can be understood through the area where snow releases, the route along which it moves and the area where it slows or deposits material. This helps explain why risk management must consider more than the point where movement begins.

  • Release area: The upper slope or snow-covered location where the unstable snow initially breaks away.
  • Track: The route through which the moving snow travels downhill.
  • Runout zone: The lower area that may be reached by the avalanche before it stops.

A building or road in the runout zone can be exposed even when its immediate surroundings appear relatively level. Valleys and channels can concentrate moving snow and associated debris.

What avalanche hazard zonation considers

Avalanche hazard assessment examines terrain, slope characteristics, past avalanche paths, snow accumulation and the potential reach of moving snow. Land-use decisions may require keeping important installations, settlements or frequently used routes away from identified dangerous paths.

Protective structures or snow-control works may be used at selected locations, but their planning and operation belong to specialist agencies. They do not justify ignoring official warnings.

Monitoring and forecasting

Forecasting combines observations of snowfall, wind, temperature and the condition of the snowpack. Weather forecasts, field observations and previous avalanche records help identify periods of greater danger. Forecasts are necessarily probabilistic because conditions can vary between nearby slopes.

In India, the Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment (DGRE), under the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), undertakes avalanche-related research, monitoring and warning work. DGRE issues avalanche warning bulletins for relevant snow-bound regions. The NDMA provides national disaster-management guidelines, while concerned administrations and infrastructure operators are responsible for implementing public safety measures in affected areas.

Precautions for residents and travellers

  • Check the applicable official avalanche warning and current road or route advisory before mountain travel.
  • Avoid avalanche-prone slopes and routes when authorities advise against movement.
  • Do not treat the absence of active snowfall as proof that the snowpack is stable.
  • Follow instructions to close roads, suspend journeys or evacuate exposed settlements.
  • Keep away from avalanche deposits and damaged infrastructure until responsible authorities confirm that access is safe.
  • Report visible avalanche activity or danger to the local administration or designated emergency service rather than approaching an unstable slope.

Public avalanche precautions are based on avoiding exposure and following official warnings. The ability to forecast regional avalanche danger does not mean that the safety of every individual snow slope can be guaranteed.

Prelims focus

  • An avalanche path includes a release area, track and runout zone.
  • The runout zone can endanger roads or settlements below the starting slope.
  • DGRE is associated with DRDO and avalanche warning work in India.
  • Snowpack conditions, snowfall, wind and temperature are relevant to avalanche forecasting.
  • Trap: A level valley floor is not automatically safe when it lies within an avalanche runout zone.

[Sources: NDMA, Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches, June 2009, sections on snow avalanche hazard, zonation, forecasting and mitigation; DRDO, Natural Hazard Management, section Avalanche Early Warning, consulted 2 November 2026; DGRE, Avalanche Warning Bulletin, 13 December 2025, snow-condition and warning information.]

pictures.alt: An avalanche moves from an upper release area down its track into a valley runout zone containing a road and buildings on level ground.
pictures.caption: Release area, track and runout zone within a single avalanche path.

title: Avalanche Hazard Zones, Warning Systems and Mountain Safety

body:
The science of combustion

A forest or grassland fire occurs when combustible vegetation begins burning and the combustion spreads beyond its initial location. The essential conditions are commonly explained through the fire triangle: fuel, oxygen and sufficient heat.

  • Fuel: Dry grass, leaves, twigs, shrubs, branches, wood and other combustible vegetation.
  • Oxygen: Supplied by the surrounding air and necessary for ordinary combustion.
  • Heat: Raises the fuel to a temperature at which ignition can occur.

The ignition temperature is the minimum temperature at which a substance catches fire under the relevant conditions. Dry vegetation generally catches fire more readily than moist vegetation because moisture absorbs heat and must be removed or heated before sustained combustion becomes easier.

Fire can be controlled by reducing available fuel, limiting oxygen or cooling the burning material, although the practical method depends on the type and scale of fire. A large vegetation fire must be managed by trained responders rather than treated as a simple household fire.

Ignition sources

Forest and grassland fires may start naturally or through human activity. Lightning is an important natural ignition source. Human-related sources include unattended fires, discarded smoking materials, agricultural burning that escapes control, sparks and deliberate ignition.

High temperature, dry weather and low humidity generally increase fire danger by drying vegetation. However, hot weather by itself does not mean that a fire will automatically ignite. An ignition mechanism and combustible material are still required.

What controls fire behaviour after ignition?

The conditions that permit ignition should be distinguished from the conditions governing how quickly and where a fire spreads. Wildland fire behaviour is strongly influenced by fuel, weather and topography.

Fuel characteristics

Fuel moisture, amount, arrangement and continuity matter. Dry grasses and leaf litter are fine fuels that can ignite and spread fire quickly. Connected patches of vegetation allow flames to travel, while gaps in combustible material may slow or interrupt spread. Larger branches and logs may burn or smoulder for longer periods.

Weather

Strong wind supplies oxygen to a burning area, bends flames towards unburnt fuel and may carry burning embers ahead of the main fire. Low relative humidity and prolonged dry conditions generally reduce fuel moisture. Rainfall often increases moisture and reduces immediate fire danger, but its effects depend on how much rain falls and the subsequent weather.

Terrain

Fire often spreads more rapidly uphill because flames and rising heat can preheat vegetation above them. Valleys, ridges and changing winds can alter fire direction. Terrain also affects the accessibility of a fire to responding personnel.

Grassland fire versus forest fire

A grassland fire spreads mainly through grasses and other low-growing vegetation. The fine, continuous fuel can allow rapid movement, especially in windy and dry conditions. A forest fire may burn fallen leaves and shrubs on the forest floor, organic matter below the surface or vegetation in tree canopies.

These terms describe the dominant vegetation and burning environment. A fire can move from grass or scrub into adjoining woodland if combustible material provides a route for spread.

Prelims focus

  • The combustion fire triangle consists of fuel, oxygen and heat.
  • Wildland fire behaviour is strongly influenced by fuel, weather and topography.
  • Dry, continuous grass can support rapid fire spread.
  • Wind may increase spread and transport burning embers.
  • Trap: Hot or dry weather increases fire danger but does not eliminate the need for ignition.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 6, Combustion and Flame, 2018–19 printing, sections 6.1–6.3; Forest Survey of India (FSI), Technical Information Series, Volume I, No. 1 (2019), section 1.1, Causes of Forest Fire; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), National Action Plan on Forest Fire, April 2018, sections on fire risk and preparedness.]

pictures.caption: Dry grasses and forest-floor vegetation burning at the edge of a dry deciduous woodland.

title: Why Forest and Grassland Fires Start and Spread
